messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arun could still recall the day his daughter Rhea was diagnosed with leukemia as if it were yesterday. She was six years old. He spent months beside her hospital bed, watching needles slide into her small arms, breathing the sharp antiseptic air, the beeping of monitors a constant soundtrack. As a bomb disposal technician, he was trained to stay calm under pressure, but here he was utterly powerless. He told himself that once she recovered, life would return to normal. It didn’t. Weeks after Rhea came home, walking into the locker room at work, a faint antiseptic smell brought the entire scene back without warning—the sterile light, the IV tubing, the sound of her crying. His heart hammered, his hands trembled, and he felt a surge of fear that made no sense in the safe space of the station. The thought followed instantly: *What’s wrong with me? I’m supposed to be the calm one.* He believed that reaction proved he was weak, and that belief itself seemed to confirm he was falling apart.

The memory never arrived as just a thought. It grabbed him by the throat, full sensory reliving that left him breathless and drenched in sweat. Each time, he was left with the sinking certainty that he had lost something permanent, that he could never be the man he was before. Sometimes the memory itself would conjure the smell of the antiseptic so vividly that he would look around the room expecting to see a hospital. His hypervigilance, the constant scanning for danger, seemed to invite more intrusions; the more he tried to stay alert, the more the memories ambushed him. On nights when his sense of threat felt unbearable—when every shadow seemed menacing—the memory of Rhea's hospital room would surface fully formed, as if the adrenaline itself had unlocked it. The physical reactions—racing heart, trembling, the feeling of being trapped—terrified him. They felt like evidence that he was going crazy, that his mind was no longer his own.

Because he saw himself as someone who couldn’t stop bad things from happening, he doubled down on vigilance. He stayed up late checking locks, listening for sounds, as if alertness alone could keep disaster away. That same belief made him sensitive to anything that could remind him of the hospital—the scent of hand sanitizer in a grocery store would catch his attention like a threat, and soon even clean air seemed menacing. At work, during a routine disposal, a sudden memory of the IV pole intruded; his hands shook just enough to make him pause. That pause saved his life, but it also convinced him that he could no longer trust himself. He stopped going to family gatherings where children were present, because seeing a child laughing would immediately transport him back to Rhea’s sickbed, and the guilt and helplessness that followed would stay for hours.

His wife grew alarmed. She found him one night standing in the kitchen at 3 a.m., rigid, unable to sleep, muttering that he had to stay alert or something terrible would happen. He told her he was losing his mind. She insisted he see someone. He finally came to therapy hoping that talking might quiet the noise in his head, but he was also afraid that admitting to weakness would make the loop tighter—that naming his fear of going crazy would only prove it was true.
